dossiers.title: Stronghold: Definitive Edition
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 9 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: Castle building balances wood, food, housing, taxes, production chains, fortifications and troop recruitment; players enjoy the patient economic planning underlying combat.
Returning players repeatedly praise how remastered art, animations, zoom options, familiar sound and music refresh the old medieval stronghold without replacing its recognizable identity.
The existing mission campaigns and added scenarios provide varied castle defense, assault and economy tasks, though some attack missions constrain tools and require slow siege tactics.
Campaign missions can be demanding and reward experimenting with productive castle layouts, but army pathfinding and constrained siege options also cause frustrating trial and error.
A recurrent complaint is the lack of offline AI skirmish and ability to add AI enemies in multiplayer; players preferring open-ended battles with bots see the omission as decisive.
Players discuss networked player-versus-player castle matches, but the absence of cooperative fights against AI limits preferred play arrangements.
A Russian player specifically praised the new campaign's Russian dubbing and respect for the original aesthetic, showing localization feedback from the launch period.
Extended interest often comes from replaying military scenarios, perfecting economies or workshop maps; players hoping for freely configurable AI battles have fewer replay options.
A launch-era Russian reviewer said that early online lag was subsequently improved; that account does not prove current multiplayer reliability.

conflicts.statement: Some returning players see a faithful and lovingly refreshed classic, while critics argue the remaster retains limiting AI behavior and omits the skirmish tools they wanted.

dossiers.title: Total War: ROME II - Emperor Edition

game_identity.work_title: Total War: ROME II - Emperor Edition

dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 9 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: Players value the grand campaign's combination of turn-based expansion, diplomacy, army upkeep and settlement development with real-time field battles commanding infantry, cavalry and siege forces.
Distinct ancient factions, victory choices and campaigns offer extensive replayability with different territorial and political development paths.
The historical setting, maps, detailed unit spectacle and soundtrack strongly appeal to Roman and classical-era history enthusiasts.
Some players find early strategic planning and diplomacy absorbing, but others criticize AI battle decisions, siege pathfinding and uneven unit balance.
Large empires and multiple campaigns sustain hundreds of hours, while repeated turns, sieges and long battle sequences can become slow or predictable.
Long-running complaints concern optional faction packs and cosmetic blood effects sold separately even though the base game is titled Emperor Edition.

A 2024 player account contrasts a buggy, poorly balanced 2013 launch with substantially better campaign performance and polish after years of updates; this is retrospective not evidence of current technical state.
A recent English Steam reviewer describes repeated crashes and some persistent interface problems, but individual testimony does not establish how widespread present-day faults are.
The title offers both cooperative campaign and competitive battles, adding opportunities to test tactics against other players; older player accounts also mention network and balance friction.

conflicts.statement: Some longtime players consider the polished, content-rich historical sandbox a series highlight, while others fault its AI, residual technical reliability and extensive paid content.

dossiers.title: DmC: Devil May Cry
dossiers.summary: Evidence summary: 9 validated structured observations; consult observations and conflicts for supported findings.

observations.statement: The responsive character-action combat mixes swords, firearms and angel/demon weapon stances into elaborate juggling combos and fast enemy crowd control; players often enjoy its accessibility.
New abilities and weapons open more combo options and challenge scores, encouraging practice and replay on harder difficulties.
Fights alternate with spectacular shifting-city traversal and platforming set pieces, though some encounters restrict effective weapons and narrow tactical freedom.
The visual art direction features surreal Limbo-city transformations and industrial/electronic music, repeatedly praised as distinctive and energetic.
Some reviewers see fluid, accessible combos as a strength; established series fans criticize reduced depth, color-restricted enemy design and bosses that are too easy.
The reboot Dante's abrasive presentation, characterization and anti-authority story polarize players: some enjoy the reinterpretation, while others reject its departure from earlier games.

Players praise the PC version's comparatively comfortable mouse-and-keyboard handling once learned, while an older Russian review reports performance problems without establishing present-day behavior.
The reasonably short campaign and combat scoring invite replays for mastery, while some players find enemy encounters tiring toward the conclusion.
A 2026 player account specifically praises combat while criticizing comparatively weak dialogue, characterization and pacing.

conflicts.statement: The same modernized, simplified combat and reimagined protagonist delight some players but frustrate series veterans who miss prior complexity and characterization.
